digital transformation of public sector institutions is a global imperative, driven by the need for greater operational efficiency, enhanced transparency, and improved citizen service delivery. In the Philippines, the foundational policy for this shift was established with the enactment of the E-Commerce Act of 2000 (Republic Act No. 8792), which aimed to facilitate the use of electronic data and documents in official and commercial transactions. However, despite the passage of the aforementioned law twenty (20) years ago, the widespread

adoption and integration of information technology (IT) for core government processes did not progress as envisioned, leading to a persistent digital divide within the bureaucracy (Placido, 2020; Information and Communications Technology Office, 2011).

policy intent and on-the-ground implementation is symptomatic of broader challenges in Philippine e-governance, including limited digital infrastructure, resistance to change, and fragmented IT initiatives (

, 2020). As a result, several key government agencies, including the Bureau of Local Government Finance Regional Office No. 2 (BLGF RO2), continue to operate with predominantly manual, paper-based systems for critical internal workflows. The BLGF RO2, as a regional office of the Bureau of Local Government

Finance under the Department of Finance, plays a crucial role in supervising local treasury operations, ensuring sound local government fiscal management, and implementing financial policies. The efficiency and security of its internal document workflows—covering memoranda, fiscal reports, policy directives, and audit documents—are therefore paramount to its regulatory and supervisory functions.

Presently, the bureau relies on a manual document routing and tracking system. This process involves physical document tracking slips, handwritten logbooks, and the personal delivery of paper files between offices and personnel. This method is inherently inefficient, prone to errors, and vulnerable to security risks. Common operational dilemmas include misplaced or lost documents, significant delays in retrieval and routing, difficulty in determining real-time document status

or location, lack of version control leading to discrepancies, and challenges in maintaining an organized audit trail for accountability (Reyes & De Leon, 2019). These inefficiencies not only consume valuable staff time and resources but also create bottlenecks that can delay financial oversight, policy implementation, and service to local government units.

The limitations of manual systems are well-documented in both academic literature and practical case studies. Research consistently shows that paper-based workflows hinder transparency, reduce productivity, and increase administrative overhead (United Nations Department of Economic and Social Affairs, 2022). Conversely, the adoption of electronic document management systems (EDMS) has been linked to significant improvements in process speed, record security, regulatory compliance, and overall organizational agility (Alavi & Leidner, 2001;
In this context, there is a critical and timely need for the BLGF RO2 to transition from its archaic
manual system to a modern, integrated digital solution. The development and implementation of a
Web-Based Document Tracking and Management Platform
for Secure and Efficient Document Workflow Automation

is proposed to directly address these challenges. Such a platform would automate the entire document lifecycle—from creation, routing, and approval to archiving and retrieval—within a secure online environment. By leveraging web technology, the platform would enable role-based access control, ensure data integrity, provide real-time tracking and notifications, and maintain a complete, tamper-evident audit log. This digital transformation aligns with the national E-Government Masterplan (EGMP) 2022 and the Philippine Development Plan 2023-2028, which prioritize the digitization of government
services to foster a resilient, inclusive, and digitally empowered society (National Economic and Development Authority, 2022).

Ultimately, this study seeks to explore the design and potential impact of such a platform for BLGF RO2. It aims to bridge the identified gap in the agency's operational capabilities by providing a framework for a system that enhances document security, streamlines workflow automation, and supports the bureau’s
mandate of promoting excellence in local government finance through modern, efficient, and transparent administrative practices.

The output of the study is a fully operational Web-Based Document Tracking and Management Platform designed to improve document routing, monitoring, and retrieval. The primary focus of this study is the design, development, and implementation of the Web-Based Document Tracking and Management Platform (WDTMP) specifically for the Bureau of Local Government Finance Regional Office No. 2 (BLGF RO2). The scope of the system is centered on automating the internal document lifecycle, which includes the digital creation of tracking profiles, real-

time routing among various divisions, and the monitoring of document status from reception to final archiving. To ensure data integrity and security, the platform incorporates role-based access control and a tamper-evident audit trail. The system allows for the attachment of digital copies in PDF formats with a predefined file size limit to support efficient storage management. Evaluation of the platform is delimited to the ISO 25010 software quality standards, focusing on functional suitability, security, and performance efficiency.

Conversely, the study is delimited in several functional areas to maintain project focus. The WDTMP is primarily a tracking and workflow automation tool; therefore, it does not function as a full-scale word processor for document creation nor as a permanent record management system for unalterable historical archives. The system requires an active internet or local network connection for real-time updates and does not support offline data synchronization. Furthermore, while the platform facilitates the routing of documents, it does not replace the physical movement of original hard copies where legal or agency policies mandate wet-ink signatures. Finally, the study focuses solely on the internal administrative workflows of BLGF RO2 and does not extend to the external public-facing portals of local government units.

at the Bureau of Local Government Finance Regional Office No. 2 (BLGF RO2) will provide substantial benefits to the following stakeholders:

This study, and the system developed from it, will significantly enhance how personnel track and monitor financial and administrative documents. It will eliminate the difficulties associated with manually locating documents and determining their status, thereby streamlining daily workflows, reducing administrative burdens, and increasing overall operational productivity.

The study and the proposed system will provide managers and supervisors with a clear, real-time overview of document processes within the office. This improved visibility will enable more informed decision-making, better resource allocation, and the identification of bottlenecks, leading to more strategic management of the bureau’s document workflow and supporting its mandate of fiscal oversight.
The Clients (Local Government Units and Stakeholders)

By automating and securing the document workflow, this web-based platform will facilitate more efficient, transparent, and accountable processing of financial documents, reports, and communications. This can lead to improved service delivery, faster response times, and greater trust in the bureau’s regulatory and support functions.

This study enhanced the researcher’s ability to design, develop, and implement a robust, well-tested software application. It also contributed significantly to the researcher’s technical expertise in system analysis, secure web development, and workflow automation within the public sector context.

This study will serve as a reference for future researchers interested in developing electronic document tracking systems or conducting comparative studies on document management and workflow automation, particularly within government financial agencies or similar bureaucratic environments.

REVIEW OF RELATED LITERATURE AND STUDIES

This chapter presents a synthesis of relevant literature, including foreign and local sources, on topics directly related to the development of a web-based document tracking and management platform designed to secure and automate document workflows.
Web-Based Document Tracking and Management Platform for Secure and Efficient Document Workflow Automation

The origins of formalized document management can be traced to the late 19th century. In 1898, Edwin Grenville Seibels patented the vertical filing cabinet, a system designed to organize loose papers in drawers within a freestanding cabinet (Grenville, 1902, as cited in Thornton, 2018). This invention marked the transition from piled desktops and bound ledgers to a searchable, categorized physical system. For decades, this model dominated offices worldwide. However, its limitations became increasingly apparent: substantial spatial demands, labor-intensive retrieval processes, and vulnerability to physical damage, loss, or deterioration (Allen, 2019).

The paradigm began to shift with the dawn of the computing age. The 1980s introduced the first significant wave of digitization. The development of affordable microcomputers and optical character recognition (OCR) scanners enabled the conversion of paper records into digital images. Early systems, often called Document Image Management (DIM), focused primarily on storage and retrieval of scanned documents. However, they were largely standalone, with minimal workflow capabilities and major challenges in version control when documents needed editing (Bannon, 1991). The true precursor to modern Electronic Document Management Systems (EDMS) emerged with the integration of document imaging with database technologies, allowing for metadata tagging and basic search functions.

A critical evolution occurred in the mid-1990s to early 2000s with the rise of the internet and client-server architecture. Systems evolved from simple image repositories to comprehensive Electronic Document Management Systems (EDMS) and Enterprise Content Management (ECM) platforms. These systems incorporated workflow engines, audit trails, and permission-based access controls. The introduction of standards like the World Wide Web Consortium’s (W3C) recommendations for web accessibility and data interchange further propelled development, allowing for more interoperable systems (Berners-Lee, 1999). The term "document" expanded beyond text and images to encompass emails, web pages, and multimedia files.

The 2010s heralded the current era of cloud-based and intelligent document management. The proliferation of Software-as-a-Service (SaaS) models made powerful EDMS accessible without significant on-premise infrastructure. This period saw the convergence of document management with Business Process Management (BPM), giving birth to sophisticated workflow automation platforms. Furthermore, the integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) introduced capabilities like automatic data extraction, smart categorization, and predictive routing, transforming passive repositories into active, intelligent components of organizational infrastructure (Davenport &

Today, the historical trajectory points toward context-aware, secure, and highly automated platforms. Modern systems are expected to ensure compliance with stringent data protection regulations (e.g., GDPR, Data Privacy Act of 2012), provide seamless mobile and remote access, and offer deep analytics on process performance. The history of document tracking is no longer just about managing files but about orchestrating knowledge, securing information assets, and automating the very pathways of organizational decision-making and service delivery

The implementation of a web-based document management platform faces significant technical, organizational, and human-centric challenges, particularly within government contexts. A primary technical challenge involves overcoming system interoperability and legacy integration issues, as new platforms must often interface with outdated proprietary systems not designed for modern API-based communication, creating data silos and migration complexities (Mergel et al., 2019). Additionally, ensuring robust data security and privacy compliance presents a formidable hurdle, requiring the platform to meet stringent national regulations such as the Data Privacy Act of 2012 while protecting sensitive information from evolving cyber threats (

Organizational resistance to change constitutes another major barrier, as employees accustomed to manual, paper-based workflows often exhibit technological aversion and digital skill gaps. This resistance can stem from a lack of familiarity, fear of job displacement, or distrust in new systems, which hinders user adoption and undermines the platform's potential impact (Venkatesh & Bala, 2022). Furthermore, sustained leadership commitment and adequate budgetary allocation are critical yet frequently unstable, as digital transformation projects compete for limited government funding and may lose priority amid shifting political agendas (Cordella & Bonina, 2022).

Infrastructure limitations, particularly in regional offices, pose a foundational challenge. Inconsistent internet connectivity and inadequate hardware can severely restrict the functionality and reliability of a cloud-based platform, exacerbating the digital divide between central and local government units (Misuraca & Viscusi, 2021). Finally, establishing standardized processes and metadata protocols across diverse departments remains a persistent difficulty, as inconsistent filing conventions and approval hierarchies can lead to disorganized digital repositories, undermining the system's searchability and auditability (Janssen et al., 2020). These multifaceted challenges necessitate a holistic implementation strategy that addresses technical, human, and institutional dimensions simultaneously.
Applied in Other Agencies or Organizations

International implementations of Web-Based Document Tracking and Management Platforms demonstrate effective strategies for secure and efficient workflow automation. In 2020, Lee and Park conducted a study of the Singapore Ministry of Finance's Digital Document Hub, which implemented a cloud-based platform using role-based workflow automation and end-to-end encryption. The system reduced document processing time by 68% and achieved 99.5% accuracy in automated routing of financial documents, validated through the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) across departmental users (Lee & Park, 2020).

In the academic sector, Thompson and Rodriguez (2022) studied the University of Cambridge Document Workflow Platform, which automates research grant documentation and administrative approvals. The system implements automated version control, electronic signature integration, and real-time collaboration features, reducing administrative overhead by 45% while improving compliance with research funding requirements. Their implementation approach emphasized phased deployment and extensive user training as critical success factors.

These international implementations collectively demonstrate that successful Web-Based Document Tracking and Management Platforms share common characteristics: cloud-based architecture for accessibility, configurable workflow automation for efficiency, multi-layered security protocols for data protection, and user-centered design for adoption. The documented outcomes—including significant reductions in processing time, improved accuracy, and enhanced security—provide a compelling evidence base for developing a similar platform for Philippine government agencies, particularly in adapting these proven approaches to local operational contexts and regulatory requirements.

Several Philippine academic institutions have pioneered the development of electronic document tracking systems, providing valuable insights for the creation of a secure and efficient workflow automation platform. The University of

the Philippines Information Technology Development Center (UP ITDC) developed a comprehensive Document Tracking System that monitors the complete document lifecycle within UP offices (UP ITDC, 2022). This system captures metadata including originating and receiving offices, personnel involved, time elapsed between departments, and supports document attachments, revisions, updates, and remarks. The implementation demonstrated how structured workflow documentation enhances institutional accountability and process transparency in academic administration.
In a notable implementation at the Southern Philippines Agri-Business and Marine and Aquatic School of Technology (SPAMAST),

et al. (2020) created a web-based document tracking system utilizing barcode technology with SMS notification capabilities. This system managed diverse document types within the Office of Records through automated status updates, significantly reducing document search time and improving response rates to document requests. Their approach demonstrated how relatively low-cost technologies can be effectively deployed to streamline document management in resource-constrained educational environments.

At Isabela State University, Echague Campus, Constantino et al. (2020) implemented an "Electronic Documents Location Tracking System" that facilitated real-time monitoring of document movement across different administrative offices. System evaluation revealed high effectiveness in streamlining document tracking processes, recording document locations, and facilitating inter-office transfers. The study emphasized user-friendly interface design and intuitive workflow navigation as critical factors for successful adoption, with users reporting significant reductions in time spent locating documents and tracking approval statuses.

These local implementations collectively demonstrate several critical success factors for document tracking systems in Philippine institutional contexts: user-centered design principles, gradual implementation strategies, appropriate technology selection based on institutional resources, and comprehensive user training programs. The documented improvements in

operational efficiency, document security, and process transparency provide compelling evidence for the potential benefits of implementing a similar Web-Based Document Tracking and Management Platform within government agencies like the BLGF, while also highlighting the importance of adapting implementation approaches to local organizational cultures and technological infrastructures.
Testing of the Efficiency of the Web-Based Document Tracking and Management Platform

The effectiveness of a Web-Based Document Tracking and Management Platform for Secure and Efficient Document Workflow Automation must be quantitatively and qualitatively assessed to validate its operational improvements. This evaluation employs statistical methods and performance metrics to measure gains in processing efficiency, security robustness, and user productivity compared to legacy manual systems.

Statistical validation of efficiency improvements utilizes the Wilcoxon Signed Rank Test, a non-parametric statistical method appropriate for analyzing paired, non-normally distributed data (McDonald, 2021). This test compares performance metrics—such as document processing time, retrieval speed, and error rates—between the traditional manual system and the new web-based platform. For instance, a study by Garcia and Lim (2022) applied this methodology in assessing a government document automation system, finding a statistically significant median reduction of 58% in approval cycle times, thereby providing empirical evidence of enhanced workflow efficiency.

A time-motion analysis framework is essential for capturing detailed efficiency metrics. This approach, as implemented in the evaluation of the National Archives of Singapore’s digital records system, involves systematically recording the duration of each workflow stage—document creation, routing, review, approval, and archiving—under both manual and automated conditions (Tan & Wong, 2023). This granular analysis identifies specific bottlenecks alleviated by automation
and provides verifiable data on time savings, directly demonstrating the platform's contribution to efficient document workflow automation.

Evaluating the platform's security posture is integral to the efficiency assessment, as robust security should not impede performance. A framework proposed by the Information Systems Audit and Control Association (ISACA, 2022) recommends measuring the security-efficiency ratio, which balances the strength of controls (e.g., encryption, access logging) against their processing overhead. For example, an audit of a provincial treasury's document system in Malaysia found that implementing AES-256 encryption added negligible latency (under 0.3 seconds per transaction) while achieving full compliance with data protection standards, proving that security and efficiency are synergistic in a well-designed platform (Abdullah & Chen, 2023).

The web-based architecture's performance under load is another critical test. Stress and scalability testing, following benchmarks set by the International Organization for Standardization’s ISO/IEC 25010 standards for software quality, assess system responsiveness, concurrent user handling, and uptime (ISO, 2021). A case study of a regional government platform in Taiwan demonstrated 99.95% availability while processing over 5,000 simultaneous document transactions, confirming that a cloud-native, web-based design is fundamental to reliable and efficient document workflow automation (Lin et al., 2022).

Finally, user-centric efficiency metrics are gathered through surveys based on the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM). Research by Santos and Ocampo (2023) on a Philippine local government unit's document system implementation showed a direct correlation between perceived ease of use, perceived usefulness, and actual reductions in task completion time. This qualitative data complements quantitative metrics, providing a holistic view of the platform's impact on operational efficiency.

In conclusion, a multi-method evaluation strategy—combining rigorous statistical testing, detailed time analysis, security auditing, system performance benchmarking, and user feedback—is necessary to conclusively prove that the Web-Based Document Tracking and Management Platform delivers on its promise

of secure and efficient document workflow automation. This evidence-based validation is crucial for stakeholder buy-in and successful adoption within the Bureau of Local Government Finance and similar agencies
ISO 25010 Software Quality Standards for Testing Compliance of the Web-Based Document Tracking and Management Platform

The development and validation of a Web-Based Document Tracking and Management Platform for Secure and Efficient Document Workflow Automation must adhere to established international standards to ensure its quality, reliability, and fitness for purpose. The ISO/IEC 25010 standard provides a comprehensive quality model that serves as the foundational framework for evaluating the system's characteristics against explicit and implicit stakeholder requirements (International Organization for Standardization [ISO], 2011). This model is pivotal for determining the specific quality attributes that define a superior software product, ensuring the final platform delivers tangible value to the Bureau of Local Government Finance (BLGF) and its clients.
The ISO 25010 model is structured into two primary dimensions: Software Product Quality and Software Quality in Use (

). The Product Quality dimension evaluates inherent properties of the software itself, while the Quality in Use dimension assesses the effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction experienced by users during real-world interaction with the system in a specific context (
et al., 2018). This dual perspective is critical for a platform whose success hinges not only on technical robustness but also on seamless adoption within a government workflow environment.

For this specific platform, the Product Quality characteristics take on targeted significance. Functional Suitability is paramount, requiring the system to provide the exact functions necessary for secure document routing, version control, and approval automation. Performance Efficiency must be rigorously tested to ensure the web-based platform handles concurrent users and large document volumes without degradation, directly supporting the goal of efficient document workflow automation. Security, as a standalone characteristic in the ISO 25010
model, is non-negotiable; the platform must demonstrate capabilities in confidentiality, integrity, non-repudiation, accountability, and authenticity to protect sensitive fiscal data (Sánchez-
& Colomo-Palacios, 2020). Furthermore, Usability and Reliability are essential to ensure the system is learnable, operable, and available when needed by government personnel.

Equally important is the Quality in Use dimension. This evaluates outcomes such as Effectiveness (can users accurately and completely achieve their document tracking goals?), Efficiency (can they do so with appropriate expenditure of resources and time?), and Satisfaction (is the user experience free from discomfort and positive in attitude?). Testing against these
metrics, as applied in a study of e-government services by Alharbi and de
(2019), ensures the platform transcends technical functionality to become a genuinely useful tool that enhances, rather than hinders, public sector productivity.

Applying this ISO 25010 framework to the evaluation of related international and local systems reveals a common thread: successful implementations are those that score highly across these interconnected quality characteristics. The documented dilemmas in traditional document management often stem from deficits in one or more of these areas—be it poor performance efficiency leading to delays, inadequate security causing data vulnerability, or low usability resulting in low adoption. Therefore, using the ISO 25010 standard as a compliance checklist and testing guide during the platform's development lifecycle is not merely an academic exercise. It is a strategic imperative to ensure the final Web-Based Document Tracking and Management Platform is engineered to a high standard of quality, capable of delivering the secure and efficient document workflow automation required to modernize government operations effectively and sustainably.

This chapter outlines the systematic approach used to develop and evaluate the WDTMP. It details the software development life cycle, the research design for performance testing, and the methods for data collection.

The researcher utilized a dual-method approach consisting of Descriptive and Developmental Research Designs to systematically address the document management challenges at BLGF RO2. The descriptive component was employed to investigate the current operational landscape, focusing on the respondents' perspectives, experiences, and the specific problems encountered within the manual document tracking system. According to

(2020), descriptive research is designed to accurately and systematically describe a population, situation, or phenomenon, which in this study involved using surveys and interviews to identify bottlenecks and security risks in the existing workflow. This baseline data provided the necessary justification for the transition to a digital platform.

For the technical creation of the system, the study applied a Developmental Research Design centered on the Systems Development Life Cycle (SDLC). As noted by Banks (2021), the SDLC provides the essential phases for creating software components that integrate into a functional, holistic system. Specifically, the researcher adopted the Sashimi Model, a methodology initiated by Peter DeGrace that blends the structured nature of the Waterfall method with the flexibility of iterative feedback. Unlike the traditional linear approach, the Sashimi Model allows for overlapping phases, enabling the researcher to identify and rectify "problem

spots" in real-time during development (Complex Tester, 2012). This model served as the primary framework for the analysis, design, development, testing, deployment, and implementation of the Web-Based Document Tracking and Management Platform (WDTMP).

The Web-Based Document Tracking and Management Platform (WDTMP) utilizes a multi-tier architecture designed to decouple the user interface, application logic, and data storage layers. This structural approach ensures the system’s scalability, high performance, and continuous availability, which are critical for the regulatory and supervisory functions of the BLGF RO2. By separating the architecture into distinct tiers—the Presentation Tier (Web Browser), the Logic Tier (Server-side processing), and the Data Tier (Database)—the platform achieves enhanced security because direct access to the database from the client-side is restricted. The Presentation Tier provides the interface for staff to access tracking profiles, while the Logic Tier, supported by DNS resolution and caching, manages the workflow rules and routing. Finally, the Data Tier handles the persistent storage of metadata and audit trails, creating an architecture that facilitates easier
maintenance and allows for future upgrades without disrupting the entire document workflow.

Figure 3.3 illustrates the functional capabilities and access levels of each user within the WDTMP to ensure a secure and efficient document workflow. The Administrator is granted full privileges to manage the overall functions of the platform, including user account management and system-wide configurations. The Management level is provided with high-level oversight, allowing them to view comprehensive statistics such as the percentage of various document types and the average turnaround time for the current year.

In contrast, the Records User and Section User are restricted to viewing statistics and document flows specific to their respective departments through localized dashboards. To ensure transparency and information dissemination across the BLGF RO2, all user levels are authorized to view formal issuances, such as Administrative Orders and Memorandum Circulars, logged into the system.
